questions.q: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
questions.fact: Copper is used in most wires because it is almost as good and much cheaper.

questions.q: Which metal is used most in electrical wires in homes?
questions.fact: Copper bends easily and carries electricity very well.

questions.q: Which metal is light and used to make soda cans?
questions.fact: Aluminum is the most common metal in Earth's crust.

questions.q: Which element is a diamond made of?
questions.fact: Pencil lead, called graphite, is made of carbon too.

questions.q: What is pencil lead actually made of?
questions.fact: Pencils never had real lead in them, the name comes from an old mix-up.

questions.q: Which element is found in computer chips and sand?
questions.fact: Silicon Valley in California got its name from the silicon chips made there.

questions.q: What do we call a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up?
questions.fact: Enzymes in your body are catalysts that help digest food.

questions.q: What is it called when a solid turns straight into a gas without melting?
questions.fact: Dry ice does this, turning from solid carbon dioxide into a foggy gas.

questions.q: What is dry ice?
choices: Ice that has been dried in the sun
questions.fact: Dry ice is about minus 78 degrees Celsius, so you should never touch it with bare hands.

questions.q: What is it called when a gas turns into a liquid?
questions.fact: Water drops on a cold drink on a hot day come from condensation.

questions.q: What is it called when a liquid turns into a solid?
questions.fact: Water is unusual because it expands when it freezes.

questions.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level, in Celsius?
questions.fact: High on a mountain, water boils at a lower temperature because the air pressure is lower.

questions.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level, in Fahrenheit?
questions.fact: Water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

questions.q: Why does ice float on water?
choices: Ice is full of air from bubbles
Water pushes it up with magnets
Ice is lighter because it is cold
Ice is less dense than liquid water
questions.fact: This is lucky for fish, because ponds freeze from the top down and the water below stays liquid.

questions.q: What is the coldest possible temperature called?
questions.fact: Absolute zero is about minus 273 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What is the fourth state of matter, found in lightning and stars?
questions.fact: Plasma is gas that is so hot that electrons get pulled off the atoms.

questions.q: What does a pH below 7 mean?
questions.fact: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2.

questions.q: What does a pH above 7 mean?
questions.fact: Soap and baking soda are bases.

questions.q: Which acid is found in lemons and oranges?
questions.fact: Citric acid gives citrus fruits their sour taste.

questions.q: Which acid is in vinegar?
questions.fact: Vinegar is mostly water with about 5 percent acetic acid.

questions.q: What happens when an acid and a base mix?
questions.fact: Antacid tablets are bases that neutralize extra stomach acid.

questions.q: What does litmus paper do?
choices: Changes color to show if something is an acid or a base
questions.fact: Acids turn blue litmus paper red, and bases turn red litmus paper blue.

questions.q: What is a mixture where one substance dissolves completely into another called?
questions.fact: Salt water is a solution of salt dissolved in water.

questions.q: Which liquid is often called the universal solvent because it dissolves so many things?
questions.fact: Water dissolves more substances than any other common liquid.

questions.q: Why do oil and water not mix?
choices: Water molecules stick to each other but not to oil
questions.fact: Oil floats on top because it is less dense than water.

questions.q: What does density measure?
choices: How much mass is packed into a space
questions.fact: A brick and a sponge can be the same size but have very different densities.

questions.q: What are the units of temperature named after a Swedish scientist?
questions.fact: Anders Celsius created his scale in 1742.

questions.q: Which temperature scale starts at absolute zero?
questions.fact: Scientists use Kelvin because it has no negative numbers.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.fact: One newton is roughly the weight of a small apple.

questions.q: What is the unit used to measure energy?
questions.fact: A joule is named after the English scientist James Prescott Joule.

questions.q: What unit is used to measure electric power?
questions.fact: A typical LED light bulb uses about 10 watts.

questions.q: What unit measures the push of electricity, like on a battery?
questions.fact: A AA battery gives about 1.5 volts.

questions.q: What unit measures electrical resistance?
questions.fact: The ohm is named after German scientist Georg Ohm.

questions.q: What unit measures how much electric current flows?
questions.fact: The ampere is often shortened to amp.

questions.q: What does hertz measure?
choices: How many times something happens per second
questions.fact: Humans can hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 hertz.

questions.q: What is the speed of light in empty space, roughly?
questions.fact: Light could circle Earth about seven and a half times in one second.

questions.q: About how fast does sound travel in air?
questions.fact: That is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder.

questions.q: Does sound travel faster in water or in air?
questions.fact: Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.

questions.q: What do we call an object breaking the sound barrier, which makes a loud boom?
questions.fact: A sonic boom happens when something goes faster than sound.

questions.q: Who was the first pilot to fly faster than the speed of sound, in 1947?
questions.fact: Chuck Yeager flew a rocket plane called the Bell X-1.

questions.q: What is an echo?
choices: A sound that gets louder by itself
A sound made by animals only
questions.fact: Bats and dolphins use echoes to find things.

questions.q: What is the loudness of sound measured in?
questions.fact: Sounds above about 85 decibels for a long time can damage your hearing.

questions.q: What do we call sounds too high-pitched for humans to hear?
questions.fact: Doctors use ultrasound to see babies before they are born.

questions.q: What do we call sounds too low-pitched for humans to hear?
questions.fact: Elephants can talk to each other using infrasound over long distances.

questions.q: What happens to light when it passes through a prism?
choices: It splits into a rainbow of colors
questions.fact: Isaac Newton used prisms to show that white light is a mix of colors.

questions.q: What are the colors of the rainbow in order?
choices: Red, yellow, blue, green, orange, purple, pink
Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
Violet, red, green, orange, yellow, blue, indigo
Blue, green, red, yellow, orange, pink, white
questions.fact: Many people remember the order with the name ROY G. BIV.

questions.q: What is the bending of light as it passes from one material into another called?
questions.fact: Refraction is why a straw in a glass of water looks broken.

questions.q: What is light bouncing off a surface called?
questions.fact: A mirror reflects almost all the light that hits it.

questions.q: What are the three primary colors of light?
questions.fact: Screens make every color by mixing tiny red, green and blue lights.

questions.q: Why does a red apple look red?
choices: It makes its own red light
It reflects red light and absorbs other colors
Red light is the only light in the room
questions.fact: Without light, nothing would have color at all.

questions.q: Why is the sky blue?
choices: Air scatters blue sunlight more than other colors
questions.fact: This scattering is called Rayleigh scattering.

questions.q: Why are sunsets often red and orange?
choices: Sunlight passes through more air, which scatters away blue light
The Sun cools down at night
questions.fact: At sunset, sunlight travels through much more of the atmosphere to reach your eyes.

questions.q: What type of light can give you a sunburn?
questions.fact: Sunscreen blocks most of the ultraviolet light that burns skin.

questions.q: What type of light can we feel as heat?
questions.fact: Night vision cameras and TV remotes use infrared light.

questions.q: Which type of wave do doctors use to see bones?
questions.fact: X-rays were discovered by Wilhelm Roentgen in 1895.

questions.q: How does a microwave oven heat food?
choices: Its waves make water molecules in the food jiggle
questions.fact: The microwave oven was invented after an engineer noticed a candy bar melted near radar equipment.

questions.q: What is the force that slows down two surfaces rubbing together?
questions.fact: Rubbing your hands together makes them warm because of friction.

questions.q: What is the force that slows things moving through air called?
questions.fact: A parachute works by creating lots of air resistance.

questions.q: What is the upward push that helps things float in water called?
questions.fact: A huge steel ship floats because it pushes aside a lot of water.

questions.q: Which Greek scientist is said to have shouted Eureka in his bath after an idea about floating?
questions.fact: Archimedes realized that the water rising in the tub could measure an object's volume.

questions.q: What does Newton's first law of motion say?
choices: Every object falls at the same speed
Objects keep doing what they are doing unless a force acts on them
questions.fact: This tendency to keep moving or stay still is called inertia.

questions.q: What does Newton's third law of motion say?
choices: Things fall at the same speed
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
questions.fact: When a rocket pushes gas down, the gas pushes the rocket up.

questions.q: According to a famous story, what fell and helped Isaac Newton think about gravity?
questions.fact: Newton himself told the apple story, but it probably did not hit him on the head.

questions.q: If you drop a bowling ball and a tennis ball at the same time with no air, which lands first?
choices: They land at the same time
questions.fact: Astronaut David Scott showed this on the Moon by dropping a hammer and a feather together.

questions.q: What is the stored energy of an object high up, like a book on a shelf, called?
questions.fact: When the book falls, its potential energy turns into kinetic energy.

questions.q: What is the energy of something that is moving called?
questions.fact: The faster something moves, the more kinetic energy it has.

questions.q: What type of energy is stored in food and batteries?
questions.fact: Your body turns the chemical energy in food into movement and heat.

questions.q: What does the law of conservation of energy say?
choices: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed
Energy only comes from the Sun
Energy is the same as mass
questions.fact: When you switch on a lamp, electrical energy changes into light and heat.

questions.q: Which simple machine is a ramp?
questions.fact: Ramps make it easier to lift heavy things by spreading the work over a longer distance.

questions.q: Which simple machine is a seesaw?
questions.fact: A lever turns around a point called a fulcrum.

questions.q: Which simple machine is used to raise a flag up a pole?
questions.fact: A pulley uses a wheel and a rope to change the direction of a pull.

questions.q: Which simple machine is an axe blade?
questions.fact: A wedge turns a downward push into a sideways push that splits things apart.

questions.q: How many classic simple machines are there?
questions.fact: They are the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge and screw.

questions.q: What is the flow of electric charge called?
questions.fact: Electric current in wires is made of moving electrons.

questions.q: What do we call a material that lets electricity flow through it easily?
questions.fact: Most metals are good conductors.

questions.q: What do we call a material that does not let electricity flow easily?
questions.fact: Rubber and plastic are good insulators, which is why wires are covered in them.

questions.q: What is a complete path that electricity flows around called?
questions.fact: If there is a break in the circuit, the electricity stops flowing.

questions.q: What is the kind of electricity that makes your hair stand up when you rub a balloon on it?
questions.fact: Lightning is a giant spark of static electricity.

questions.q: What do opposite magnetic poles do?
questions.fact: Two north poles or two south poles push each other away.

questions.q: What does a compass needle point toward?
questions.fact: A compass works because the needle is a tiny magnet.

questions.q: What do we call a magnet made by running electricity through a coil of wire?
questions.fact: Junkyards use giant electromagnets to lift cars, then switch them off to drop them.

questions.q: Who flew a kite in a storm to show that lightning is electricity, according to a famous story?
questions.fact: Franklin later invented the lightning rod to protect buildings.

questions.q: Who made the first electric battery around 1800?
questions.fact: The unit volt is named after him.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered that moving a magnet near a wire makes electricity?
questions.fact: This idea is how power plants and generators make electricity today.

questions.q: Which inventor is famous for developing alternating current power systems and the Tesla coil?
questions.fact: The car company Tesla is named after him.

questions.q: What does a light bulb's thin wire, called a filament, do when electricity flows through it?
questions.fact: LED bulbs do not use filaments and waste much less energy as heat.

questions.q: What does LED stand for?
questions.fact: LEDs can last tens of thousands of hours.

questions.q: What is Einstein's most famous equation?
questions.fact: It shows that a tiny bit of mass can turn into a huge amount of energy.

questions.q: What is the main kind of energy that nuclear power plants use?
questions.fact: Splitting heavy atoms is called nuclear fission.

questions.q: Which energy source is renewable?
questions.fact: Renewable energy comes from sources that will not run out, like sunlight and wind.

questions.q: Which fossil fuel is a black rock formed from ancient plants?
questions.fact: Coal formed from swamp plants that were buried for millions of years.

questions.q: What do we call energy that comes from the heat inside the Earth?
questions.fact: Iceland gets much of its electricity and heat from geothermal energy.

questions.q: What do we call electricity made from flowing water at dams?
questions.fact: Hydropower has long been one of the world's biggest sources of renewable electricity.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies living things called?
questions.fact: Biology comes from Greek words meaning the study of life.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies matter and energy called?
questions.fact: Famous physicists include Isaac Newton and Albert Einstein.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies plants called?
questions.fact: Botanists have described hundreds of thousands of plant species.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies animals called?
questions.fact: Zoologists may work in zoos, labs or out in the wild.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies tiny germs like bacteria called?
questions.fact: Microbiologists help develop medicines and vaccines.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies dinosaur fossils called?
questions.fact: Archaeologists study things made by people, not dinosaurs.

questions.q: What is the basic unit of all living things?
questions.fact: Some living things, like bacteria, are made of just one cell.

questions.q: Who first named the cell after looking at cork under a microscope in 1665?
questions.fact: Hooke thought the tiny boxes in cork looked like small rooms called cells.

questions.q: Which scientist made very strong early microscopes and first saw bacteria?
questions.fact: Leeuwenhoek called the tiny creatures he saw animalcules.

questions.q: What part of a cell holds its DNA in plants and animals?
questions.fact: The nucleus is often called the cell's control center.

questions.q: Which part of a plant cell captures sunlight to make food?
questions.fact: Chloroplasts are green because they contain chlorophyll.

questions.q: Which part of a cell is often called its powerhouse?
questions.fact: Mitochondria turn food into energy the cell can use.

questions.q: What do plant cells have that animal cells do not?
questions.fact: The stiff cell wall helps plants stand up straight.

questions.q: What does DNA stand for?
questions.fact: DNA carries the instructions for building and running a living thing.

questions.q: What shape is a DNA molecule?
questions.fact: A double helix looks like a twisted ladder.

questions.q: Which scientist's X-ray photo of DNA helped show its double helix shape?
questions.fact: Her famous image is known as Photo 51.

questions.q: Which two scientists described the double helix model of DNA in 1953?
questions.fact: Their model was built using data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.

questions.q: Who is known as the father of genetics for his experiments with pea plants?
questions.fact: Mendel was a monk who grew thousands of pea plants in his garden.

questions.q: What are the sections of DNA that carry instructions for traits like eye color called?
questions.fact: Humans have about 20,000 genes.

questions.q: Who came up with the theory of evolution by natural selection?
questions.fact: Alfred Russel Wallace came up with the same idea around the same time.

questions.q: On which islands did Charles Darwin study finches and giant tortoises?
questions.fact: Darwin visited the Galapagos in 1835 on a ship called HMS Beagle.

questions.q: Which scientist created the system of giving every living thing a two-part Latin name?
questions.fact: Linnaeus published his naming system in the 1700s and named thousands of plants and animals himself.

questions.q: What is the scientific name for humans?
questions.fact: Homo sapiens means wise human in Latin.

questions.q: What are the largest groups that scientists sort living things into, like animals, plants and fungi?
questions.fact: Below kingdom come phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.

questions.q: Which kingdom do mushrooms belong to?
questions.fact: Fungi cannot make their own food from sunlight, so they are not plants.

questions.q: Which tiny living things are made of a single cell with no nucleus?
questions.fact: There are more bacteria in your body than there are people on Earth.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic, in 1928?
questions.fact: Fleming noticed mold had killed bacteria in a dish he forgot to clean.

questions.q: What do antibiotics kill?
questions.fact: Antibiotics do not work on viruses, like the ones that cause colds.

questions.q: Which scientist invented a way to heat milk to kill germs?
questions.fact: The process is called pasteurization after him.

questions.q: Who made the first vaccine, for smallpox, in 1796?
questions.fact: Jenner used material from cowpox, and the word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

questions.q: Which disease became the first human disease to be completely wiped out by vaccines?
questions.fact: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

questions.q: Who developed the first successful polio vaccine in the 1950s?
questions.fact: Jonas Salk chose not to patent the vaccine so it could reach more people.

questions.q: What is a virus?
choices: A tiny germ that can only multiply inside living cells
questions.fact: Viruses are much smaller than bacteria and need a microscope called an electron microscope to see.

questions.q: What do plants release into the air during photosynthesis?
questions.fact: Most of the oxygen we breathe came from plants and tiny ocean algae.

questions.q: What green substance in leaves captures sunlight?
questions.fact: In autumn, chlorophyll breaks down and the yellow and orange colors in leaves show through.

questions.q: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.fact: Some tree roots spread much wider than the tree's branches.

questions.q: What are the tiny holes on leaves that let gases in and out called?
questions.fact: A single leaf can have thousands of stomata.

questions.q: What is it called when water evaporates out of a plant's leaves?
questions.fact: A big tree can release hundreds of liters of water into the air on a hot day.

questions.q: What is it called when a seed starts to grow?
questions.fact: Seeds need water, air and the right temperature to germinate.

questions.q: What is it called when pollen moves from one flower to another?
questions.fact: Bees, butterflies, birds, bats and even the wind can pollinate flowers.

questions.q: What part of a flower makes pollen?
questions.fact: The pollen is made in a part at the top of the stamen called the anther.

questions.q: Which tree is the tallest kind in the world?
questions.fact: A coast redwood named Hyperion is over 115 meters tall, as of 2025 the tallest known tree.

questions.q: Which kind of tree is the largest by volume?
questions.fact: A giant sequoia named General Sherman is the largest single-stem tree on Earth by volume.

questions.q: Which plant catches and digests insects with snapping leaves?
questions.fact: The trap only snaps shut if tiny trigger hairs are touched twice quickly.

questions.q: Which fast-growing plant is actually a type of grass?
questions.fact: Some bamboo can grow almost a meter in a single day.

questions.q: What do cactuses have instead of regular leaves to save water?
questions.fact: Cactus stems are green and do the photosynthesis instead of the leaves.

questions.q: How can you tell a tree's age after it is cut down?
questions.fact: Each ring usually stands for one year of growth.

questions.q: What is the world's largest flower?
questions.fact: Rafflesia flowers can be about 1 meter wide and smell like rotting meat.

questions.q: Which plant has a tall stalk and a giant, smelly bloom and is called the corpse flower?
questions.fact: The titan arum may bloom only once every several years, and people line up to see and smell it.

questions.q: What is the name for the chain showing who eats whom in nature?
questions.fact: A food chain might go from grass to a rabbit to a fox.

questions.q: In a food chain, what are plants called because they make their own food?
questions.fact: Almost every food chain on Earth starts with energy from the Sun.

questions.q: What do we call living things like fungi and worms that break down dead plants and animals?
questions.fact: Decomposers return nutrients to the soil so new plants can grow.

questions.q: What is an ecosystem?
choices: Living things and their surroundings working together
questions.fact: A pond, a forest and a coral reef are all ecosystems.

questions.q: What is it called when two different living things help each other?
questions.fact: Bees get nectar from flowers, and flowers get their pollen spread by bees.

questions.q: What is a species that is brought to a new place and harms the plants and animals there called?
questions.fact: Cane toads were brought to Australia in 1935 and spread across much of the country.

questions.q: What is the variety of all the different living things in a place called?
questions.fact: Tropical rainforests have some of the highest biodiversity on Earth.

questions.q: What is the step-by-step way scientists test ideas called?
questions.fact: It includes asking a question, making a guess, testing it and looking at the results.

questions.q: What is a scientist's testable guess called?
questions.fact: A good hypothesis can be shown to be wrong by an experiment.

questions.q: In an experiment, what is the one thing you change on purpose called?
questions.fact: The thing you measure to see what happens is called the dependent variable.

questions.q: What tool makes tiny things look much bigger?
questions.fact: Some electron microscopes can show individual atoms.

questions.q: What tool measures temperature?
questions.fact: The first thermometers were made in the 1600s.

questions.q: What tool measures air pressure?
questions.fact: Falling air pressure on a barometer often means stormy weather is coming.

questions.q: What tool measures mass in a science lab?
questions.fact: A balance compares an object's mass with known masses.

questions.q: What glass container with straight sides and a spout is used to hold liquids in a lab?
questions.fact: Beakers have lines on the side to give a rough measurement of volume.

questions.q: What shallow round dish with a lid is used to grow bacteria in a lab?
questions.fact: It is named after German scientist Julius Petri.

questions.q: What should you wear to protect your eyes during a science experiment?
questions.fact: Even simple experiments can splash liquids into eyes.

questions.q: What is a lever's turning point called?
questions.fact: Archimedes said that with a long enough lever he could move the world.

questions.q: What is the unit used to measure frequency, like radio stations?
questions.fact: Heinrich Hertz proved radio waves exist in the 1880s.

questions.q: How many centimeters are in a meter?
questions.fact: The meter was once defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.

questions.q: What metric unit is used to measure the volume of a liquid?
questions.fact: One liter of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram.

questions.q: What does mass measure?
choices: How much matter is in an object
questions.fact: Your mass stays the same on the Moon, but your weight changes.

questions.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
choices: Weight is the pull of gravity on mass
Mass changes on the Moon but weight does not
questions.fact: On the Moon you would weigh about one sixth as much but have the same mass.

questions.q: What is speed?
choices: How far something travels in a certain time
questions.fact: Speed is distance divided by time.

questions.q: What is acceleration?
choices: A change in speed or direction
questions.fact: When a car speeds up, slows down or turns, it is accelerating.

questions.q: What force pulls objects toward the center of the Earth?
questions.fact: Gravity is the weakest of nature's basic forces, but it acts over huge distances.

questions.q: Why does a feather fall more slowly than a rock on Earth?
choices: Rocks are pushed by the wind
Air resistance slows the feather more
questions.fact: In a vacuum, a feather and a rock fall at exactly the same speed.

questions.q: What is the pulling force in a stretched rope or string called?
questions.fact: Tug-of-war is a battle of tension in a rope.

questions.q: What does a lens that is thicker in the middle do to light?
questions.fact: Magnifying glasses use this kind of lens, called a convex lens.

questions.q: Why do you see lightning before you hear thunder?
choices: Light travels much faster than sound
Your eyes are closer to the storm
questions.fact: Counting the seconds between them and dividing by 3 gives the distance in kilometers.

questions.q: What causes thunder?
choices: Air heated by lightning expanding very fast
questions.fact: Lightning can heat the air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, hotter than the Sun's surface.

questions.q: What do we call heat moving through a solid, like a metal spoon in hot soup?
questions.fact: Metals are good conductors of heat, which is why pot handles are often made of plastic or wood.

questions.q: What do we call heat moving by warm liquid or gas rising and cool sinking?
questions.fact: Convection is why the upstairs of a house is often warmer than the downstairs.

questions.q: How does heat from the Sun reach Earth through empty space?
questions.fact: Radiation can travel through a vacuum because it does not need any material.

questions.q: What color clothing keeps you coolest in strong sunshine?
questions.fact: White reflects most light, while black absorbs it and gets warm.

questions.q: What does a thermos bottle use to keep drinks hot or cold?
questions.fact: Without air in between, heat cannot easily move by conduction or convection.

questions.q: What makes a rainbow appear in the sky?
choices: Sunlight bending and reflecting in raindrops
questions.fact: To see a rainbow, the Sun must be behind you.

questions.q: What is the word for how high or low a sound is?
questions.fact: Short, tight guitar strings make higher pitches.

questions.q: What is sound?
questions.fact: When you talk, your vocal cords vibrate and shake the air.

questions.q: What part of a guitar vibrates to make sound?
questions.fact: The hollow body makes the sound louder.

questions.q: What does a laser make?
choices: A narrow, powerful beam of light
questions.fact: The word laser started as an abbreviation of light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered radioactivity in uranium in 1896?
questions.fact: He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie and Pierre Curie.

questions.q: Which two elements did Marie and Pierre Curie discover?
questions.fact: Marie named polonium after her home country, Poland.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus?
questions.fact: Rutherford shot tiny particles at gold foil and some bounced right back.

questions.q: Which scientist proposed in the early 1800s that all matter is made of atoms?
questions.fact: The idea of atoms goes back to ancient Greece, but Dalton turned it into modern science.

questions.q: Who is often called the father of modern chemistry?
questions.fact: Lavoisier showed that burning needs oxygen and helped name it.

questions.q: Who invented the light bulb that became popular in homes in 1879?
questions.fact: Other inventors made earlier bulbs, but Edison's team made one that lasted long and was practical.

questions.q: Who discovered that white light is made of all the colors?
questions.fact: Newton passed sunlight through a prism and then recombined the colors back into white light.

questions.q: Which famous scientist was born in Germany and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921?
questions.fact: Einstein won it for explaining the photoelectric effect, not for relativity.

questions.q: Which scientist wrote the book Silent Spring about the dangers of pesticides?
questions.fact: The book helped start the modern environmental movement.

questions.q: Which scientist and inventor was known as the Wizard of Menlo Park?
questions.fact: Edison's lab in Menlo Park, New Jersey, was one of the first research labs.

questions.q: Which scientist is famous for his work with peanuts and helping farmers rotate crops?
questions.fact: Carver found hundreds of uses for peanuts and sweet potatoes.

questions.q: What award, started by a Swedish inventor of dynamite, honors great scientists?
questions.fact: Alfred Nobel left his fortune to create the prizes, first given in 1901.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.fact: Marie Curie won in 1903 for physics and again in 1911 for chemistry.

questions.q: What is the opposite of a vacuum, where air is squeezed tightly together?
questions.fact: Car tires hold air at high pressure to support the car's weight.

questions.q: What happens to the air pressure as you climb a tall mountain?
questions.fact: That is why your ears pop on mountain roads and airplanes.

questions.q: Why does a sealed bag of chips puff up when you take it up a mountain?
choices: The air pressure outside is lower
questions.fact: The air inside the bag pushes out harder than the thinner air outside.

questions.q: What is the name for how much water vapor is in the air?
questions.fact: High humidity makes hot days feel even hotter because sweat evaporates slowly.

questions.q: What is the scientific word for the temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas?
questions.fact: Each pure substance has its own boiling point.

questions.q: Why do people put salt on icy roads?
choices: Salt soaks up all the water
Salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes
questions.fact: Salt water must get colder than fresh water to freeze.

questions.q: What happens to most materials when they are heated?
questions.fact: Bridges have gaps called expansion joints so they can grow in summer heat.

questions.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
questions.fact: In a chemical change, new substances are made that were not there before.

questions.q: Which of these is a physical change?
questions.fact: In a physical change, the substance stays the same, it just changes form.

questions.q: What gas do we need for fire to burn?
questions.fact: A fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen, called the fire triangle.

questions.q: Why do some fire extinguishers use carbon dioxide?
choices: It pushes away the oxygen a fire needs
questions.fact: Covering a small pan fire with a lid works the same way, by cutting off oxygen.

questions.q: What gives fireworks their bright colors?
questions.fact: Strontium makes red, copper makes blue, and barium makes green.

questions.q: Which element do all living things contain, making life carbon-based?
questions.fact: Carbon atoms can link together in chains and rings, making millions of different molecules.

questions.q: What is the most common element in the human body by mass?
questions.fact: Your body is mostly water, and oxygen makes up most of water's mass.

questions.q: What is the most common element in the universe?
questions.fact: About three quarters of all normal matter in the universe is hydrogen.

questions.q: Which shiny metal never rusts or tarnishes and is often used in jewelry?
questions.fact: Gold is so stretchy that one gram can be pulled into a wire more than 2 kilometers long.

questions.q: What is an alloy?
choices: A mix of a metal with other elements
questions.fact: Steel is an alloy made mostly of iron and a little carbon.

questions.q: Which alloy is made from copper and tin?
questions.fact: Bronze was so important that a whole period of human history is called the Bronze Age.

questions.q: Which alloy is made from copper and zinc?
questions.fact: Many trumpets and trombones are made of brass.

questions.q: Which metal is added to steel to make stainless steel that resists rust?
questions.fact: The chromium forms a thin invisible layer that protects the steel.

questions.q: What are plastics mostly made from?
questions.fact: Most plastics take hundreds of years to break down.

questions.q: What is glass mostly made from?
questions.fact: Sand is heated to over 1,500 degrees Celsius to melt it into glass.

questions.q: Which natural material comes from the sap of rubber trees?
questions.fact: Latex is made into natural rubber for things like balloons and gloves.

questions.q: What is the name of the strong, stretchy material invented in 1935 and used for stockings and ropes?
questions.fact: Nylon was the first fully synthetic fiber to become a big success.

questions.q: What is the name for tiny pieces of plastic smaller than 5 millimeters?
questions.fact: Microplastics have been found from the deep ocean to mountaintops.

questions.q: What is a magnet strongest at?
questions.fact: You can see this by sprinkling iron filings around a bar magnet.

questions.q: Which metal is NOT attracted to a magnet?
questions.fact: That is why magnets do not stick to soda cans.

questions.q: What is a lodestone?
questions.fact: People used lodestones to make the first compasses.

questions.q: What simple viewer uses a tiny hole to safely project the Sun's image onto paper?
questions.fact: A pinhole projector lets you see the Sun's image on a piece of paper.

questions.q: What does a periscope use to let you see over things?
questions.fact: Submarines used periscopes to look above the water while staying hidden.

questions.q: What is the name for the study of sound?
questions.fact: Concert halls are carefully designed using acoustics.

questions.q: What is the study of light called?
questions.fact: Glasses, cameras and microscopes all depend on optics.

questions.q: What is the study of heat and energy called?
questions.fact: Thermo comes from the Greek word for heat.

questions.q: What is the study of how air moves around objects, like airplane wings?
questions.fact: Race cars use aerodynamics to stay pressed down onto the track.

questions.q: What helps an airplane wing create lift?
choices: Its shape makes air push it upward
questions.fact: The wing's shape and tilt turn the passing air downward, and the air pushes the wing up in return.

questions.q: What do hydraulic machines, like car brakes and diggers, use to work?
questions.fact: Liquids are hard to squeeze, so they pass a push along very well.

questions.q: What is a chemical reaction that gives off heat called?
questions.fact: Burning wood and hand warmers are exothermic reactions.

questions.q: What is a chemical reaction that takes in heat and feels cold called?
questions.fact: Instant cold packs use endothermic reactions.

questions.q: What is burning called in science?
questions.fact: Combustion needs fuel, oxygen and heat.

questions.q: What is the gas that makes soda fizzy?
questions.fact: Soda is bottled under pressure to keep the carbon dioxide dissolved.

questions.q: What is the name for the earthy smell of rain falling on dry ground?
questions.fact: Part of the smell comes from a chemical made by bacteria in soil.

questions.q: What do we call substances made of two or more elements chemically joined?
questions.fact: Water and table salt are both compounds.

questions.q: What do you call particles in water that make it cloudy and settle over time?
questions.fact: Muddy water is a suspension, so the mud slowly sinks to the bottom.

questions.q: How do you separate salt from salt water?
questions.fact: When the water evaporates, the salt crystals are left behind.

questions.q: What can you use to separate iron filings from sand?
questions.fact: The magnet pulls the iron and leaves the sand behind.

questions.q: Which way of separating mixtures uses paper to separate colors in ink?
questions.fact: Black marker ink often splits into several colors in chromatography.

questions.q: What is the process of boiling a liquid and collecting the cooled vapor called?
questions.fact: Distillation can turn salty seawater into fresh drinking water.

questions.q: What is the smallest unit of an element that still has its properties?
questions.fact: It would take hundreds of thousands of atoms lined up in a row to cross the width of a human hair.

questions.q: Which particles make up protons and neutrons?
questions.fact: The name quark came from a line in a novel by James Joyce.

questions.q: What are tiny packets of light energy called?
questions.fact: Photons have no mass and always travel at the speed of light.

questions.q: What is the name of the huge particle accelerator under the border of France and Switzerland?
questions.fact: Its main ring is about 27 kilometers around.

questions.q: Which particle, sometimes called the God particle, was found at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012?
questions.fact: Peter Higgs predicted it back in 1964 and won a Nobel Prize in 2013.

questions.q: What is the half-life of a radioactive substance?
choices: The time for half of it to decay
questions.fact: Carbon-14's half-life of about 5,730 years helps scientists date ancient things.

questions.q: How do scientists find the age of old bones and wood from living things?
questions.fact: Carbon dating works for things up to about 50,000 years old.

questions.q: What is the device that turns movement into electricity, used in power plants?
questions.fact: A motor does the opposite, turning electricity into movement.

questions.q: What device changes electricity into motion in things like fans and toys?
questions.fact: Electric motors work using magnets and coils of wire.

questions.q: What safety device in a home breaks a circuit when too much current flows?
questions.fact: Older homes used fuses, which melt to break the circuit.

questions.q: Why should you never touch electrical outlets with wet hands?
choices: Water helps electricity flow into your body
questions.fact: Pure water does not conduct well, but tap water has dissolved minerals that do.

questions.q: What does a solar cell turn sunlight into?
questions.fact: Solar cells are mostly made from silicon.

questions.q: What does a wind turbine turn into electricity?
questions.fact: Some wind turbine blades are more than 100 meters long.

questions.q: What is the energy that comes from the rise and fall of the ocean called?
questions.fact: Tidal energy is very predictable because tides follow the Moon.

questions.q: What are the three main fossil fuels?
questions.fact: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide into the air.

questions.q: What is the main gas in natural gas?
questions.fact: Gas companies add a smelly chemical so people can notice leaks, because methane has no smell.

questions.q: What kind of energy does a stretched rubber band store?
questions.fact: When you let go, the stored energy turns into motion.

questions.q: What is a perpetual motion machine?
choices: An impossible machine that would run forever without energy
questions.fact: It breaks the laws of physics because some energy is always lost as heat.

questions.q: What is the scientific study of weather called?
questions.fact: Meteorologists use satellites, balloons and computers to forecast weather.

questions.q: What do we call the temperature at which a solid melts?
questions.fact: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Which state of matter has a fixed shape and fixed volume?
questions.fact: The particles in a solid are packed tightly and only vibrate in place.

questions.q: Which state of matter has no fixed shape but a fixed volume?
questions.fact: A liquid takes the shape of whatever container it is in.

questions.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
questions.fact: Gas particles move fast and spread far apart.

questions.q: What is a non-Newtonian fluid, like cornstarch mixed with water?
choices: A gas that turns to ice
A liquid that acts like a solid when squeezed fast
questions.fact: You can punch a pool of cornstarch slime and it feels hard, but your hand sinks if you push slowly.

questions.q: What makes a boomerang come back?
choices: The shape of its spinning wings
questions.fact: A boomerang's arms work like spinning airplane wings that make it turn.

questions.q: Which force keeps you from flying off a spinning merry-go-round?
questions.fact: Without that inward pull, you would move off in a straight line.

questions.q: What is the name for the curved path of a thrown ball?
questions.fact: Gravity pulls the ball down as it moves forward, curving its path.

questions.q: What is inertia?
choices: An object's resistance to changing its motion
questions.fact: Seat belts protect you because inertia keeps your body moving when a car stops suddenly.

questions.q: What is momentum?
questions.fact: A slow, heavy truck can have more momentum than a fast bicycle.

questions.q: What instrument measures the strength of electric current?
questions.fact: An ammeter measures current in amperes.

questions.q: Which planet's name is also the name of an element on the periodic table?
questions.fact: Uranium, neptunium and plutonium are named after planets and a dwarf planet too.

questions.q: Which element is named after Albert Einstein?
questions.fact: Einsteinium was first found in the debris of a hydrogen bomb test in 1952.

questions.q: Which element is named after Marie Curie and Pierre Curie?
questions.fact: Curium was first made in a lab in 1944.

questions.q: What tiny living thing is yeast?
questions.fact: Yeast is a single-celled fungus that people have used for baking for thousands of years.

questions.q: Why do cut apples turn brown?
choices: Chemicals in the apple react with oxygen in the air
questions.fact: Lemon juice slows the browning because its acid gets in the way of the reaction.

questions.q: Why does popcorn pop?
choices: Water inside the kernel turns to steam and bursts it
questions.fact: The steam builds up pressure until the hard hull cracks open.

questions.q: What happens to the particles of a substance when it is heated?
questions.fact: Temperature is really a measure of how fast particles are moving.

questions.q: What is a crystal?
choices: A solid with atoms arranged in a repeating pattern
questions.fact: Salt and sugar grains are tiny crystals.

questions.q: What forms when water vapor freezes directly onto cold surfaces?
questions.fact: Frost forms on clear, cold nights when surfaces get colder than freezing.

questions.q: Which liquid has a higher boiling point, salt water or fresh water?
questions.fact: Dissolved salt makes water boil at a slightly higher temperature.

questions.q: What is sugar made of?
questions.fact: Table sugar's scientific name is sucrose.

questions.q: What is the main gas in the bubbles when you boil water?
questions.fact: The big bubbles in boiling water are pockets of steam.

questions.q: What happens when you mix the primary paint colors red and blue?
questions.fact: Paints mix differently from light because they absorb colors instead of giving them off.

questions.q: What color do you get by mixing red and green light?
questions.fact: This is how screens show yellow, by lighting red and green pixels together.

questions.q: What color do you see when all colors of light are mixed together?
questions.fact: White light, like sunlight, is a mix of all the colors.

questions.q: What color is an object that absorbs all colors of light?
questions.fact: Black objects get hot in the sun because they absorb so much light.

questions.q: What do you call a material that lets light pass straight through, like clear glass?
questions.fact: Wax paper is translucent, letting some light through, and wood is opaque.

questions.q: What do you call a material that blocks all light, like wood?
questions.fact: Shadows form when an opaque object blocks light.

questions.q: What happens to your shadow as the Sun gets lower in the sky?
questions.fact: Your shadow is shortest around midday, when the Sun is highest.

questions.q: Why does a spoon look bent in a glass of water?
choices: The glass is curved like a mirror
Light bends as it moves from water into air
questions.fact: This bending of light is called refraction.

questions.q: What does a concave mirror, curved inward like a spoon, do to light?
questions.fact: Car headlights and big telescopes use curved mirrors.

questions.q: Why do you see yourself upside down in the bowl of a shiny spoon?
choices: The curved surface flips the reflection
It is a trick of the metal
questions.fact: On the back of the spoon, the curve bulges out and your reflection is right side up.

questions.q: What tool can show the parts of an onion skin cell?
questions.fact: Iodine stain is often added to make the cell parts easier to see.

questions.q: What is the jelly-like fluid that fills a cell called?
questions.fact: Many of the cell's chemical reactions happen in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: What is the thin outer layer that controls what enters and leaves an animal cell?
questions.fact: The membrane lets some things in and keeps others out.

questions.q: What large storage sac holds water in plant cells?
questions.fact: When a plant's vacuoles lose water, the plant wilts.

questions.q: What is the process where one cell splits into two cells called?
questions.fact: Your body makes millions of new cells every second through cell division.

questions.q: What do we call living things made of only one cell?
questions.fact: Amoebas and most bacteria are unicellular.

questions.q: Which tiny water creature moves by changing its shape and stretching out false feet?
questions.fact: The amoeba's false feet are called pseudopods.

questions.q: What do we call a group of similar cells working together, like muscle?
questions.fact: Tissues group together to make organs.

questions.q: Which are the four groups of molecules that build all living things?
choices: Carbohydrates, fats, proteins and nucleic acids
questions.fact: Nucleic acids include DNA and RNA.

questions.q: What does a seed need to start growing?
questions.fact: Most seeds do not need light to germinate, but the young plant soon needs light to grow.

questions.q: What do roots, stems and leaves of a plant have inside to carry water?
questions.fact: Another set of tubes, called phloem, carries sugar made in the leaves.

questions.q: What is the female part of a flower that receives pollen?
questions.fact: The sticky top of the pistil, called the stigma, catches pollen grains.

questions.q: What do flowers turn into after pollination?
questions.fact: Anything with seeds inside, like a tomato or a pumpkin, is a fruit to a scientist.

questions.q: Why do sunflowers turn to face the Sun when they are young?
questions.fact: Grown-up sunflowers usually stop moving and face east.

questions.q: What is a plant's growth toward light called?
questions.fact: Houseplants on a windowsill often lean toward the window.

questions.q: Which part of a plant holds it up and carries water to the leaves?
questions.fact: Tree trunks are big, woody stems.

questions.q: Which plants reproduce with spores instead of seeds?
questions.fact: Look under a fern's leaves for brown spots, which hold the spores.

questions.q: What do plants need from soil besides water?
questions.fact: Fertilizers add minerals like nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium to soil.

questions.q: What are the long-lasting traces of a living thing preserved in rock studied in science called?
questions.fact: Most fossils form when a living thing is buried quickly in mud or sand.

questions.q: What do we call a change in a gene that can create a new trait?
questions.fact: Most mutations are tiny and have no effect, but some lead to new features over many generations.

questions.q: What is it called when a living thing has a body part or behavior that helps it survive?
questions.fact: A polar bear's thick fur is an adaptation to the cold.

questions.q: What is a clone?
choices: A living thing with the exact same DNA as another
questions.fact: Dolly the sheep, born in 1996, was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

questions.q: What is the name of the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, born in 1996?
questions.fact: Dolly was named after the singer Dolly Parton.

questions.q: What do we call the study of how traits are passed from parents to children?
questions.fact: Traits like dimples and freckles can run in families.

questions.q: What do we call germs that cause disease?
questions.fact: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites can all be pathogens.

questions.q: Why should you wash your hands with soap?
choices: Soap breaks up oils and lifts germs away
questions.fact: Scrubbing for at least 20 seconds helps remove germs.

questions.q: What is the tiny eight-legged creature that lives in pillows and eats dead skin flakes?
questions.fact: Dust mites are too small to see without a microscope.

questions.q: What do we call bacteria that live in your gut and help you digest food?
questions.fact: Your gut is home to trillions of microbes.

questions.q: Which organism glows in some ocean waves at night, making the water sparkle blue?
questions.fact: When waves stir them, these tiny organisms flash blue light.

questions.q: What is bioluminescence?
questions.fact: Fireflies, anglerfish and some mushrooms are bioluminescent.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist who studies the chemicals in living things?
questions.fact: Biochemists helped discover how medicines work inside the body.

questions.q: What does a seismograph measure?
questions.fact: It draws wiggly lines that show how strong the shaking was.

questions.q: What is a hypothesis called once it has been tested many times and explains lots of facts?
questions.fact: In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation, not just a hunch.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a renewable resource?
questions.fact: Coal takes millions of years to form, so we use it much faster than nature can replace it.

questions.q: What does recycling aluminum cans save compared with making new aluminum?
questions.fact: A recycled can can be back on a store shelf in about two months.

questions.q: What is the greenhouse effect?
choices: Plants growing faster in glass houses
Gases in the air trapping heat near Earth's surface
questions.fact: Without any greenhouse effect, Earth would be too cold for most life.

questions.q: Which gas from burning fuels is the main cause of recent global warming?
questions.fact: As of 2025, carbon dioxide levels in the air are higher than at any time in human history.

questions.q: Which gas, produced by cows burping, is a strong greenhouse gas?
questions.fact: Methane traps much more heat than carbon dioxide, though it stays in the air for less time.

questions.q: Which scientist suggested that heavier objects do not fall faster than lighter ones, against what Aristotle taught?
questions.fact: Aristotle had taught that heavy objects fall faster, and people believed it for nearly 2,000 years.

questions.q: Who explained in a 1687 book that the gravity that makes apples fall also keeps the Moon in orbit?
questions.fact: The book is often called the Principia.

questions.q: Whose improvements to the steam engine helped power the Industrial Revolution?
questions.fact: The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

questions.q: Which inventor sent the first radio signals across the Atlantic Ocean in 1901?
questions.fact: Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.q: Who invented the code of dots and dashes used to send telegraph messages?
questions.fact: In Morse code, SOS is three dots, three dashes and three dots.

questions.q: Who invented dynamite in 1867?
questions.fact: Nobel used his fortune to create the Nobel Prizes.

questions.q: Which scientist came up with a famous thought experiment about a cat in a box?
questions.fact: The thought experiment was meant to show how strange quantum physics seems.

questions.q: What branch of physics studies the behavior of super tiny things like atoms and electrons?
questions.fact: In quantum physics, particles can act like waves.

questions.q: What is the name for a scientist's careful record of what they see during an experiment?
questions.fact: Good scientists write down everything, even results they did not expect.

questions.q: Why do scientists repeat experiments?
choices: To make sure the results are reliable
questions.fact: If others can repeat an experiment and get the same result, it is much more trustworthy.

questions.q: What do we call the amount of space something takes up?
questions.fact: You can find the volume of an odd-shaped rock by seeing how much water it pushes up in a measuring cup.

questions.q: What does a kilogram measure?
questions.fact: Since 2019, the kilogram has been defined using a number from physics instead of a metal cylinder kept in France.

questions.q: What is the metric prefix that means one thousand, as in kilometer?
questions.fact: Milli means one thousandth, so a millimeter is a thousandth of a meter.

questions.q: Which metric prefix means one millionth?
questions.fact: A micrometer is a millionth of a meter, about the size of some bacteria.

questions.q: What is the name of the tiny unit used to measure atoms and very small things, a billionth of a meter?
questions.fact: Your fingernails grow about one nanometer every second.

questions.q: Which element is a soft metal that explodes when dropped in water?
questions.fact: Sodium is stored under oil to keep it away from water and air.

questions.q: Which gas is lighter than helium but very flammable?
questions.fact: The airship Hindenburg was filled with hydrogen and burned in 1937.

questions.q: What gas did early airships like the Hindenburg use to float?
questions.fact: Modern blimps use helium instead, because it does not burn.

questions.q: Which element is a yellow solid that smells like rotten eggs when it burns or reacts?
questions.fact: Rotten eggs smell because they give off a gas made of sulfur and hydrogen.

questions.q: Which element glows in the dark and was discovered in urine in 1669?
questions.fact: Hennig Brand found it while trying to make gold.

questions.q: Which radioactive element is used as fuel in most nuclear power plants?
questions.fact: A small pellet of uranium fuel can make as much energy as about a ton of coal.

questions.q: Which element is added to toothpaste to help prevent tooth decay?
questions.fact: It is added as fluoride, which makes tooth enamel stronger.

questions.q: Which element is used in many rechargeable batteries in phones and laptops?
questions.fact: Lithium is the lightest metal of all.

questions.q: Which is the heaviest naturally common element of these?
questions.fact: Uranium has 92 protons in each atom.

questions.q: What is the densest naturally occurring element?
questions.fact: A small ball of osmium is about twice as heavy as the same size ball of lead.

questions.q: How do scientists name new elements?
choices: After the year they were found
After places, scientists, myths or properties
questions.fact: The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry approves the names.

questions.q: What are the gases in the far right column of the periodic table called?
questions.fact: Noble gases hardly react with anything.

questions.q: What are the very reactive metals in the first column of the periodic table called?
questions.fact: The farther down the column you go, the more violently they react with water.

questions.q: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.fact: The Sun is about 150 million kilometers away, much closer than any other star.

questions.q: Which star is the closest to our Sun?
questions.fact: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away, so its light takes over four years to reach us.

questions.q: What is the brightest star in the night sky?
questions.fact: Sirius is nicknamed the Dog Star because it sits in the constellation Canis Major, the Great Dog.

questions.q: Which star stays almost still in the sky above Earth's North Pole?
questions.fact: Polaris, the North Star, has helped travelers find north for hundreds of years.

questions.q: What two gases make up most of the Sun?
questions.fact: About three quarters of the Sun's mass is hydrogen.

questions.q: What process makes the Sun shine?
questions.fact: In the Sun's core, hydrogen atoms smash together to make helium and release huge amounts of energy.

questions.q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.fact: If the Sun suddenly vanished, we would not notice for about 8 minutes.

questions.q: What type of star is the Sun?
questions.fact: Even though it is called a dwarf, the Sun is bigger than most stars in the Milky Way.

questions.q: What is the visible surface of the Sun called?
questions.fact: The photosphere is about 5,500 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What is the Sun's thin outer atmosphere, seen glowing during a total solar eclipse, called?
questions.fact: The corona is over a million degrees, far hotter than the Sun's surface, and scientists are still studying why.

questions.q: What are the darker, cooler patches on the Sun's surface called?
questions.fact: Sunspots are caused by strong magnetic fields, and some are bigger than Earth.

questions.q: What happens during a solar eclipse?
questions.fact: A total solar eclipse can turn day into twilight for a few minutes.

questions.q: What happens during a lunar eclipse?
choices: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The Moon passes behind the Sun
questions.fact: During a total lunar eclipse the Moon often turns a coppery red, which is why people call it a blood moon.

questions.q: Why does the Moon shine at night?
questions.fact: The Moon's surface is actually a dark gray, a bit like old asphalt.

questions.q: About how long does the Moon take to orbit Earth?
questions.fact: The Moon takes about 27.3 days to orbit Earth, but about 29.5 days to go from one full moon to the next.

questions.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
choices: It does not spin at all
It spins once for each trip around Earth
The other side is too dark to see
questions.fact: This is called tidal locking, and many moons in the solar system do it.

questions.q: What are the big, flat, dark areas on the Moon called?
questions.fact: Early astronomers thought these dark plains were seas, so they named them maria, which is Latin for seas.

questions.q: Which mission was the first to land people on the Moon?
questions.fact: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969.

questions.q: Who was the second person to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the Moon about 19 minutes after Neil Armstrong.

questions.q: Which Apollo 11 astronaut stayed in orbit around the Moon while the others landed?
questions.fact: Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia alone around the Moon.

questions.q: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module that landed on the Moon?
questions.fact: When it touched down, Neil Armstrong radioed that the Eagle has landed.

questions.q: Which Apollo mission had an oxygen tank explode on the way to the Moon?
questions.fact: The crew could not land, but they looped around the Moon and made it home safely.

questions.q: How many people have walked on the Moon?
questions.fact: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972.

questions.q: Which Apollo mission was the last to land on the Moon?
questions.fact: Apollo 17 landed in December 1972, and no one has walked on the Moon since.

questions.q: Which mission was the first to carry astronauts around the Moon?
questions.fact: The Apollo 8 crew took the famous Earthrise photo on Christmas Eve 1968.

questions.q: What did astronauts drive on the Moon during the last three Apollo missions?
questions.fact: The three lunar rovers were left behind and are still parked on the Moon.

questions.q: Which country launched the first artificial satellite?
questions.fact: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957, starting the Space Race.

questions.q: What was the name of the dog that orbited Earth aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957?
questions.fact: Laika was a stray dog from the streets of Moscow.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to travel into space?
questions.fact: Valentina Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times aboard Vostok 6 in 1963.

questions.q: Who was the first American woman in space?
questions.fact: Sally Ride flew aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger in 1983.

questions.q: Who was the first American to orbit Earth?
questions.fact: John Glenn circled Earth three times in Friendship 7 in 1962.

questions.q: Who was the first American to travel into space?
questions.fact: Alan Shepard later hit golf balls on the Moon during Apollo 14.

questions.q: Who was the first person to go on a spacewalk?
questions.fact: Alexei Leonov floated outside his spacecraft for about 12 minutes in 1965.

questions.q: What was the name of Yuri Gagarin's spacecraft?
questions.fact: Yuri Gagarin's flight on April 12, 1961, lasted about 108 minutes.

questions.q: What does NASA stand for?
questions.fact: NASA studies flight in the air (aeronautics) as well as space.

questions.q: In what year was NASA created?
questions.fact: NASA was created in 1958, less than a year after Sputnik 1 launched.

questions.q: Which space station have astronauts lived on without a break since the year 2000?
questions.fact: People have lived on the International Space Station continuously since November 2000.

questions.q: About how long does the International Space Station take to circle Earth once?
questions.fact: That means astronauts on board see about 16 sunrises every day.

questions.q: About how high above Earth does the International Space Station orbit?
questions.fact: That is roughly the distance from New York City to Washington, DC.

questions.q: About how fast does the International Space Station travel?
questions.fact: At that speed, it could cross the whole United States in about 10 minutes.

questions.q: Which Soviet and Russian space station orbited Earth from 1986 to 2001?
questions.fact: Mir means peace or world in Russian.

questions.q: What was the name of America's first space station, launched in 1973?
questions.fact: Skylab fell back to Earth in 1979, and some pieces landed in Western Australia.
